cases.title: Route 32 widening: two workers killed at a Limón 2000 roundabout
cases.place: National Route 32, Route 4 junction at the Frío river to Puerto Limón, Limón province, Costa Rica
cases.point: The Limón end of the corridor. The coordinate is the point AidData gives for that end of the route in record 37364 (OpenStreetMap 9.9919, -83.0248). The two deaths of 6 November 2025 were at a roundabout near the Limón 2000 entrance on the edge of Limón; no source gives a coordinate for that roundabout. The widening runs the 107 km from the Route 4 junction at the Frío river to Puerto Limón's district centre (AidData records 37364 and 39847), so the point stands for the corridor and not for a site.

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: Two financing agreements signed with the Government of Costa Rica on 3 June 2013, worth $396 million together, for the rehabilitation and extension of National Route 32 between the Route 4 junction and Limón: a US$296 million buyer's credit, loan number 1420202052013211015, at 4% over 20 years with a 5-year grace period and a 0.25% commitment fee and a 0.25% management fee (AidData record 37364), and a government concessional loan of RMB 628 million at 2% over 20 years with a 5-year grace period on the same fees (AidData record 39847). Both records give the commitment date as 3 June 2013 and the actual start as 20 November 2017. Law 9293 ratified the two agreements; AidData's record says the Costa Rican government approved them on 10 March 2015, while the account of the finance minister's appearance before the Legislative Assembly's Limón commission says the law was approved in February 2015 (Semanario Universidad, 2 November 2023). AidData also records that the China-Latin America Finance Database, co-produced by the Inter-American Dialogue and Boston University, treats the project as a single $395 million loan rather than two.

cases.conditions: The two loans were to cover 85% of a US$465,593,387.06 engineering, procurement and construction contract, CONAVI-CHEC-00, between Costa Rica's National Road Council and China Harbour Engineering Company, signed the same day as the loans (AidData record 37364). The expropriations and the relocation of public services were to be paid by a national counterpart rather than by the loans. Three figures are published for that counterpart, each at its own date: $69 million within a $465 million investment on the day the start order was given (La República, 20 November 2017); more than $55 million within a cost then put at more than $521 million (CRHoy, 24 October 2022); and almost $90 million, as the finance minister told the Limón commission (Semanario Universidad, 2 November 2023).

companies.name: China Harbour Engineering Company Ltd. (CHEC)
companies.role: Engineering, procurement and construction contractor, ordered to start work by CONAVI on 20 November 2017. Teletica and La Teja report the two men killed on 6 November 2025 as CHEC workers, La Teja quoting a surviving colleague who names the company; El Observador reported the same day that the victims wore vests bearing the MOPT insignia but were not the ministry's own staff, being employed by a company that provided a service to it, and named no employer.
companies.desc: Chinese contractor for ports, dredging, land reclamation, roads and railways, and a subsidiary of China Communications Construction Company (CCCC). AidData record 37364 lists it as the project's implementing state-owned company.

companies.name: Consejo Nacional de Vialidad (CONAVI)
companies.role: Borrower's implementing body, responsible for the expropriations and for the contract with CHEC. The Constitutional Chamber's judgment 2025-29197 orders CONAVI's executive director, with the public works minister, to carry out Lanamme's recommendations on the roundabouts within a year.
companies.desc: The National Road Council, a body under Costa Rica's Ministry of Public Works and Transport that builds and maintains the national road network. Expropriation files pass to the ministry's Real Estate Acquisition Directorate (DABI).

cases.community: Two workers on the widening were killed at about 6 a.m. on Thursday 6 November 2025 at a roundabout near the Limón 2000 entrance, when a trailer overturned and the container it carried fell on a group of workers. The Traffic Police said the driver appeared to have been speeding (CRHoy, 6 and 7 November 2025). A surviving colleague, Roberto Barrantes, said the group had arrived by truck minutes earlier to work on the widening, that the trailer was travelling fast and failed to take the turn and struck the wall, and that the two men who died were having breakfast with their backs to the road; he was hurt on the ribs, an ankle and the nape (La Teja, 7 November 2025). The number hurt is given two ways: four seriously injured (Teletica, 6 November 2025) and six injured (CRHoy, 6 November 2025). Hauliers and residents quoted the same day blamed the roundabouts built along the route rather than the driver, one of them saying the construction was badly done (Teletica). The roundabouts replaced the grade separations and interchanges in the original design: the government decided on the substitution in 2023, arguing lower cost and faster work, and the public works ministry described the roundabouts in an April 2025 statement as functional and safe (CRHoy, 6 November 2025). On 12 September 2025 the Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court granted an amparo against the public works ministry and CONAVI over safety deficiencies in the roundabouts between the Sarapiquí junction and Limón, in judgment 2025-29197, and ordered the minister and CONAVI's executive director to implement the technical measures and recommendations of the University of Costa Rica's National Laboratory of Materials and Structural Models (Lanamme) within a year; the amparo was brought by a Limón resident, Marco Vinicio Levy Virgo (Delfino, 18 September 2025). Lanamme's report to the court found that the roundabouts meet the contract's parameters but do not reach the minimum diameters set by international standards and that the studies give no sufficient technical justification for using them instead of the grade separations (Delfino; CRHoy). The Comptroller General's report said the temporary roundabouts added by the last addenda to the contract do not meet the technical requirements for heavy trucks and were designed for 20 kilometres an hour and for light vehicles, that Lanamme and the Directorate General of Traffic Engineering had both warned of poor visibility and reduced turning radii, and that the road was still running on temporary solutions with no financial plan for the definitive grade separations (Comptroller General's report, reported by Teletica, 11 September 2026). The expropriations ran behind the works throughout. The finance minister, Nogui Acosta, listed the works having been started without the expropriations ready among the project's problems, at the Legislative Assembly's special Limón commission (Semanario Universidad, 2 November 2023). The published counts of what was required fall over time: about 1,400 properties, with about 700 cases of people occupying the right of way, on the day the start order was given (La República, 20 November 2017); about 700 after the project was limited to the existing right of way, the executing unit told La República on 27 November 2019; 637 required, with 182 plots, 28.57%, in the State's hands, another 164 entered into possession voluntarily under agreements with their owners while payment was being formalised, and 606 of the 637 files already lodged with DABI, in CONAVI's executive works report 48 with a September 2022 cut-off (CRHoy, 24 October 2022); 581 required with 238 in the State's name, per the finance minister in November 2023 (Semanario Universidad); 569 required with 345 completed and 245 in process at a March count, then 496 required with 362 registered and 134 pending, in the UN Office for Project Services report reported by La Nación on 8 August 2024, which also recorded that the ministry had dropped at least 73 expropriations after the roundabout redesign and that in some cases money already deposited for owners with the Attorney General's office had to be returned; and 515 files handled, 408 of them effective, 107 still in process with 67 of those carrying voluntary entries into possession that had not been made effective, and 475 plots, 92%, available to work on with 19 awaiting demolition, in the same office's report with a 31 March cut-off reported by La Nación on 9 May 2025. The Comptroller General put the number of expropriation files CONAVI ordered dropped at 74 and said the decision had to be reversed after warnings from the Attorney General's office (Teletica, 11 September 2026).
cases.suppression: Residents of Limón province demonstrated against the roundabouts in October and November 2024. At a press conference in November 2024 the president, Rodrigo Chaves, called the movement political and said it was “16 gatos”, sixteen cats, the then public works minister Mauricio Batalla said the group wanted to mess the government about, and Chaves said he would apply the law against people who protested against the roundabouts (CRHoy, 6 November 2025, recounting the earlier exchanges).
cases.killed_note: Two: René Marquetti, a Cuban worker who had been in Costa Rica about two months and working for the company about a month, and Didier García Brenes, 53, of Jicaral de Puntarenas, whose first name La Teja spells Diddier, who had been working on Route 32 for about 20 days. Both were crushed by a container that fell from an overturning trailer at a roundabout near the Limón 2000 entrance on the morning of Thursday 6 November 2025, while they were with a work group on the widening; CRHoy and La Teja report them as workers on those works and La Teja names CHEC as their employer. The cause is given two ways on the day: the Traffic Police said the trailer driver appeared to have been speeding, and hauliers and residents quoted by Teletica blamed the roundabouts' geometry. The Judicial Investigation Organisation was investigating. No document ties the two deaths to the roundabout design; the Constitutional Chamber's judgment of 12 September 2025 and Lanamme's report predate the accident and are about the roundabouts' safety, not about it.
cases.displaced_note: No document counts people or households moved. The expropriation counts are of plots and files, not of people: 164 plots entered into possession under agreements with their owners while payment was being formalised at September 2022, and 67 voluntary entries into possession not made effective at the 31 March cut-off reported in May 2025. No source names an owner left unpaid or gives a sum owed.
cases.outcome: CHEC claimed US$25 million from CONAVI in 2022, saying right of way had not been handed over on time in some sections and citing cost increases from inflation; the public works minister, Luis Amador, said the country was not in a position to take on more cost, and that the State had broken its promise to complete the expropriation procedures in four months (CRHoy, 24 October 2022). Design and construction stood at 71.65% against 89.33% planned at the end of September 2022 (CONAVI works report 48, via CRHoy) and at 84.3% physical progress at September 2023, when the finance minister put the cost at US$552.5 million against US$485.6 million originally and completion at December 2024 against September 2020 (Semanario Universidad, 2 November 2023). AidData's record says 91.85% of the project was complete as of December 2024, with a target completion date of 28 May 2025. The head of the executing unit said in early May 2025 that the four lanes of the main trunk along the 104 km between the Rio Frío junction and the centre of Limón would be functional in October, with minor works and details to follow (La Nación, 9 May 2025). The Comptroller General's report, which came after the CHEC contract expired and the executing unit was dissolved in April, ordered the ministry and CONAVI to submit within 30 days a plan for road safety and for the works left unfinished (Teletica, 11 September 2026).

cases.confidence_note: The two deaths are reported by four Costa Rican outlets on 6 and 7 November 2025, two of which put the dead men on CHEC's payroll, and the roundabout findings come from a Constitutional Chamber judgment, a University of Costa Rica laboratory report to that court and the Comptroller General's report: none of them is the lender's. Three things are left open. The number hurt is four seriously injured in Teletica and six injured in CRHoy. The employer is CHEC in Teletica and La Teja, while El Observador says the victims wore the ministry's vests and worked for a company contracted to the ministry, which it does not name. And no document connects the trailer's overturning to the roundabout design: the Traffic Police gave speeding as the apparent cause on the day, hauliers and residents blamed the roundabouts, and the court judgment and the laboratory report, both earlier, go to the roundabouts' safety in general. On the expropriations, no source names an owner left unpaid or gives a sum owed, and the counts of what was required fall over the project's life for two stated reasons: the project was limited to the existing right of way in 2019, and the 2023 redesign to roundabouts dropped at least 73 files, 74 in the Comptroller General's count, a decision the Attorney General's office then made the ministry reverse.
cases.whole: The project widens 107 km of National Route 32 from two lanes to four between the Route 4 junction at the Frío river and Puerto Limón's district centre, the road that carries most of Costa Rica's foreign trade to the ports of Moin and Limón; AidData's records put 80% of the country's exports and imports through those ports. The cost rose from US$485.6 million to US$552.5 million and completion moved from September 2020 to December 2024, the finance minister told the Legislative Assembly's Limón commission (Semanario Universidad, 2 November 2023). The grade separations and interchanges in the original design were replaced by roundabouts from 2023; the Constitutional Chamber ordered the measures Lanamme recommended for them carried out within a year on 12 September 2025, and the Comptroller General found in 2026 that the road was still running on the temporary roundabouts with no financial plan for the definitive crossings.
